## Houlihan Lokey Finds Size-Weighted Defaults in Private Credit Nearly Doubled in the Third Quarter, Reaching a Near-Term High With Smaller Borrowers the Most Impacted


November 19, 2026


**· Across the full market, defaults rose to 1.5% of outstanding loan principal from 0.8% the quarter before, with healthcare and consumer sectors seeing the most stress. Companies with less than $100 million of EBITDA saw defaults rise to 3.9% compared with 3.0% in the second quarter.**


**·** **Borrowers with EBITDA below $20 million experience a wider range of outcomes and greater earnings volatility, leading to underperformance compared with larger issuers. Loans in this cohort valued below 90% of par have risen from roughly 1% in 2023 to 11% today.**


**·** **Borrowers with $20 million to $100 million of EBITDA continue to show signs of increasing stress; borrowers above $100 million remain the least impacted.**


LOS ANGELES--(BUSINESS WIRE)--


Houlihan Lokey, Inc. (NYSE:HLI), the global investment bank, found that default rates among private credit borrowers nearly doubled in the third quarter of 2026, increasing to 1.5% of outstanding loan principal compared with 0.8% in the second quarter, according to Houlihan Lokey’s Private Credit DataBank. By count, defaults among all borrowers increased to 3.7% compared with 2.5% in the prior quarter. Defaults among borrowers with less than $100 million of EBITDA, the bulk of the direct lending market, ran at 3.9% on a size-weighted basis and 5.0% by count in the third quarter of 2026, up from 3.0% and 3.6% in the second quarter. Default occurrences are disproportionately concentrated among borrowers with less than $100 million of EBITDA. This divergence reinforces that default risk in private credit remains closely associated with borrower scale. The largest companies are continuing to perform, while lower- and core-middle-market borrowers are defaulting at meaningfully higher rates. These figures are based on the DataBank’s most fundamental definition of default, which captures technical defaults as well as payment defaults.


Higher observed earnings volatility is contributing to smaller borrower underperformance. Lower middle-market borrowers with between $10 million and $20 million of EBITDA are more volatile than larger borrowers, with 35% of borrowers in this cohort growing EBITDA by more than 25% since origination, compared with 28% in the core middle market. However, the downside is almost as pronounced, with 18% of small borrowers having lost more than 25% of EBITDA, more than double the 8% observed in the core middle market. Lenders are responding by adjusting underwriting discipline. In recent years, small-borrower deals have been originated at lower leverage levels. 2025 and 2026 vintages closed at a median leverage of 4.3x and 3.8x, respectively, compared with 4.6x for 2021 and prior loans. Through the first nine months of 2026, leverage ratios at underwriting came in a full turn below those of the core middle market.


By sector, stress remains concentrated rather than widespread. Healthcare again had the highest default rates, at 7.1% by count and 4.6% on a size-weighted basis, concentrated among provider platforms built through acquisition. Consumer followed at 4.6% by count and 2.5% on a size-weighted basis.


“Default levels rose again in the third quarter, but the stress is not evenly spread. The largest companies continue to perform, while borrowers with less than $100 million of EBITDA are showing meaningfully more strain,” said Dr. Cindy Ma, Managing Director and Global Head of Portfolio Valuation and Fund Advisory Services at Houlihan Lokey. “Borrowers in the lower middle market have the widest swings in earnings, leading to higher default rates. Lenders appear to be tightening underwriting standards for the smallest companies in response. We will continue to monitor these trends closely, as the divide by borrower size is likely to shape credit performance in the quarters ahead.”


Loan valuations tell a similar story. Marks generally stabilized quarter over quarter, yet 7% of all loans remain valued below 90% of par, more than double the historical average. The picture varies sharply by size, with the lower middle market being the weakest cohort. Among borrowers with $10 million to $20 million of EBITDA, the share marked below 90% of par stands at 11%, up from roughly 1% in 2023. Stress continues to build in the core middle market: 6% of loans to borrowers with $20 million to $100 million of EBITDA are marked below 90% of par, the highest level in the past three years. By contrast, just 2% of loans to borrowers with more than $100 million of EBITDA are valued below that threshold.


Borrower fundamentals continued to grow overall. Median revenue rose 5.9%, and median EBITDA rose 8.1% year over year, with 70% of borrowers growing revenue and 66% growing EBITDA. Most borrowers continue to perform at or near their highest observed revenue and EBITDA levels. 85% are at or within 10% of peak revenue, and roughly two-thirds or more are within that range in terms of EBITDA and enterprise value. When underperformance is observed, it is more common in EBITDA and enterprise value than in revenue, pointing to margin and valuation multiple pressure rather than weaker demand.


Borrower interest coverage slipped in the third quarter, with the median falling to 1.68x in September from 1.73x in June, the first decline since mid-2025, even as median EBITDA grew 8.1%. The share of borrowers with coverage below 1.0x rose to 15.1% from 13.9%. Interest coverage sensitivities show coverage is more dependent on earnings than rates: A 100 bps rise in base rates would lower median coverage to 1.55x and lift the sub-1.0x share to 18.0%, while a 25% decline in EBITDA at current rates would cut the median to 1.26x and double the sub-1.0x share to 30.0%.


“Fundamentals remain healthy, with median EBITDA up 8.1% year over year and most borrowers at or near peak performance, but higher financing costs are starting to have an impact,” said Timothy Kang, Managing Director in Houlihan Lokey’s Portfolio Valuation and Fund Advisory Services practice. “The Federal Reserve’s recent rate hike and possible future rate hikes could continue to weigh on interest coverage and further expose the weakest borrowers.”


Software, the sector attracting the most investor attention amid the debate over AI disruption, continued to record strong operating performance. Financial results remain ahead of where they stood at origination: Median revenue is 24% higher, and median EBITDA is 10% higher than they were when the loans first closed. Software defaults remained among the lowest at 1.0% on a size-weighted basis, reflecting strong trailing performance. Valuations, meanwhile, are forward-looking and incorporate more conservative multiple assumptions than at underwriting, given observed movement in public comparable company multiples.


“As a leading provider of private credit valuation services, Houlihan Lokey has a unique view of the market,” said Chris Cessna, Managing Director in Houlihan Lokey’s Portfolio Valuation and Fund Advisory Services practice. “Due to the depth and scale of our practice, we are able to draw proprietary insights from the loan and portfolio company metrics that we capture. As a result, our clients are better informed and can act with more confidence.”


The findings are drawn from Houlihan Lokey’s Q3 2026 Private Credit DataBank Market Trends & Insights report, which is available to clients of the firm.


**About the Private Credit DataBank**


Houlihan Lokey’s Private Credit DataBank is a proprietary dataset and analytics platform delivering structured, loan-level insights into the private credit market. Built from the firm’s private credit valuation work, the DataBank includes datasets and observations dating back to 2017 and is refreshed every quarter. Each loan carries more than 300 standardized data fields spanning terms, covenants, fair value metrics, credit metrics, and borrower financials. Coverage spans the full direct lending market, from borrowers with less than $20 million of EBITDA to those with more than $100 million, across industries, geographies, and capital structures.
